speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: asked 	the Minister for National Development (a) whether there is any correlation or increase in neighbour disputes with regard to the number of occupants living in a HDB unit over the past five years; (b) whether the Ministry foresees that the increased rental occupancy cap for HDB units from January 2024 will result in more of such disputes; and (c) if so, how will HDB intervene to manage it.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: asked the Minister for National Development whether HDB will limit the number of flats in each HDB block that will be allowed to house up to eight unrelated people under the new occupancy guidelines in order to ensure the existing infrastructure such as lift operations and bicycle parking space can cope with increased density of occupants in the block.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I invite the Member to seek clarifications if need be.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If the question has been addressed, it may not be necessary for him to proceed with the question for future Sittings.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Since 2022, we have seen sharp increases in rents in both the public and private rental market.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Prior to the pandemic, rents had stayed broadly stable, even a bit soft.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, COVID-19 caused unprecedented disruption in the construction industry, global supply chains and border controls, and the ensuing construction delays contributed to significant tightness in our rental market.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In addition to the supply-side constraints, the delays resulted in strong rental demand from Singaporeans who were seeking interim housing while awaiting the completion of their new residential units.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Subsequently, with the easing of border restrictions in 2022, non-resident rental demand also quickly recovered.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To address these supply and demand imbalances, we have undertaken a broad suite of measures to support households that intend to rent.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes significantly ramping up our public and private housing supply and increasing the supply of flats available under the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) for those awaiting completion of their new Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Public and private housing rents have showed recent signs of stabilising, with the quarterly increase in public and private housing rents moderating to 1.9% and 0.8% respectively in the third quarter of 2023, from 3% and 2.8% respectively in the previous quarter.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: That said, we expect rental demand to remain robust over the near term.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: That is why we announced the temporary relaxation of the occupancy cap for 4-room and larger HDB flats, and private residential properties of at least 90 square metres.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Allowing larger units to be rented out to more tenants will increase rental supply, even as we recognise that not all landlords and tenants will tap on the relaxed occupancy cap.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: By increasing supply, we aim to ease the pressure in the rental market and help to moderate rents overall.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will benefit all households seeking to rent, such as Singaporean families who are in-between homes, including those waiting for the completion of their new flats, as well as Work Pass holders who play a critical role in our domestic economy and essential services, such as healthcare workers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As of November 2023, there are approximately 58,000 HDB whole flats that are rented out.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is about 5% of the approximately one million sold HDB flats islandwide.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Of these, 16% are rented out to six unrelated occupants.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: About 90% of these occupants are non-residents, with most in their 20s or 40s.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Some Members have raised concerns about infringements of the occupancy cap and potential disamenities that may arise from this temporary relaxation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have put in place measures to mitigate these infringements and disamenities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, HDB regulates who is allowed to rent a HDB flat or a bedroom to minimise disamenities and maintain the Singaporean character of our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have put in place the non-citizen quota of 8% for HDB neighbourhoods and 11% for HDB blocks, which limits the number of flats that can be rented to foreigners in each neighbourhood and block.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Non-Malaysian Work Permit holders from the construction, marine and process sectors are also not permitted to rent HDB flats or bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: A Member asked if we intend to limit the number of flats in an HDB block that may tap on the temporarily relaxed occupancy cap, to prevent overloading of existing infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: While we do not currently have plans to impose such a cap, the existing non-citizen quota will help to limit the increase in occupants in each block, given that most of those renting at the occupancy cap are non-citizens.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, HDB flat owners are required to seek HDB’s approval prior to renting out their flats or bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: HDB also undertakes routine inspections to ensure that owners and tenants comply with the terms and conditions of approval and do not cause serious disamenities to the public.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Over the past five years, instances of feedback relating to nuisance caused by tenants renting HDB flats or bedrooms constituted 1.5% of the total feedback on nuisance from neighbours.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Where friction arises between neighbours, including tenants, HDB adopts a mediative approach and advises flat owners and tenants to be mindful of causing disturbances to others.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Should the parties require additional mediative assistance, we will encourage them to tap on Government initiatives, such as the inter-agency Community Dispute Management Framework and the Community Mediation Centre, which provide facilitated mediation sessions that can help parties reach mutually acceptable solutions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Over the past five years, HDB has taken action against an average of 115 cases of unauthorised renting a year, including cases where flat owners had breached the occupancy cap.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As we temporarily relax the occupancy cap, we will continue to take firm action against those who breach the rules.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Depending on the severity of the infringement, HDB will issue written warnings, impose financial penalties or compulsorily acquire the flat for the most severe cases.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the event of serious disamenities, the authorisation will cease, requiring the property to revert to its original occupancy cap of six.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: URA undertakes regular inspections to ensure compliance with the prevailing occupancy cap.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Those who breach the cap can be fined and/or imprisoned.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I understand of course there is a need to meet the increasing accommodation needs nationally to address the increasing housing needs of both locals and foreign non-home owners in this very tight rental market.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And, of course, looking at the number of questions, many Members of Parliament have had to handle disputes over the years primarily between the transient tenants and the neighbours who own their homes permanently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, where tenants are non-citizens, are there more specific, more blatant, explicit measures to ensure that they are familiar with local standards in terms of safety, in terms of noise or even the use of these units as Airbnb type of accommodation or practices like unlawful partitions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Are there blatant, explicit measures to ensure they understand?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Number two, to ensure that the units do not turn out to be unregulated hostels, causing a negative impact on both the occupants and the neighbours, what are some measures that can be done to proactively prevent this from happening?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I believe these are at the back of the minds of many Members when they raise the questions today about potential disamenities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We do not have a feel of how many of the full tenants and landlords will take advantage of this temporary relaxation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will take all feedback and complaints seriously and we will investigate and take firm action if needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: URA, likewise, has been maintaining a high enforcement tempo over the last five years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On average, there were about 330 instances each year where enforcement actions were taken.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I assure Members that we will take all feedback and complaints seriously; and we take firm action if needed.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I guess it is never easy whenever it comes to neighbourly disputes and we all know we have received such feedback.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Trying to do that mediator role is probably one of the most challenging.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: I have got three supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The first one is, back in 2018, the Ministry made the decision to reduce the number from nine to six in terms of the occupancy cap.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: There are always questions: while this is a temporary measure, why is the number increased back to eight and not nine?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The second one is, given the very robust rental demand at present – and that is the reason for this temporary measure – would the Ministry have sufficient capacity to do the enforcement to make sure that the landlords stick within the number that has been put as a cap?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: And lastly, given the disamenities that have been happening, there is still a lot – particularly, noise between neighbours – that we have still not resolved, even with the current limitations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: What is HDB's plan on trying to manage the situation?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Sometimes, it is not enough to just tell them to go for mediation through the Community Medication Centre.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Would the Senior Minister of State elaborate on this?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At that point in time, we revised the occupancy cap from nine to six for HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Her question was, why not nine; go back the original number?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For us, we will continue monitoring whether this move will help to elevate the rental tightness that we currently face and also, some of the consequences in terms of potential disamenities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I think we will continue reviewing the results of this move and we will continue to look and see whether this relaxation will continue.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The second question is about whether we have enough resources to enforce.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is something we take seriously, and we will take the adequate steps to make sure that we follow up on feedback, complaints and to continue the tempo of inspections and enforcements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The third supplementary question, if I got it correctly as I was scribbling it down, is about noise disamenities and what are the steps that we can take.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Well, Sir, firstly, let me set the context.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The number of feedback relating to neighbourly disputes as a result of rental, is about 1.5% of the total feedback received about nuisance from neighbours.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, by and large, I would believe that most of the tenants and landlords are responsible in making sure they are aligned and consistent with the norms and culture in our HDB estates.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The second point is that issues around noise disamenities go way beyond just about rental units.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It goes into many of the other aspects because tolerance levels and sensitivity to noise are actually a very complex and multi-faceted issue, and we have had many discussions about this issue in this House.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Suffice to say that these are issues that we continue to take seriously and work together with community partners through the different mechanisms to minimise neighbourly disputes and to still take a mediative approach in the first instance.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will request every Member to keep your supplementary question short.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just two short supplementary questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is relating to the number of rental flats that are being rented out right now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And the context is really that, given that there is an increased number of units completing, a lot of them will still be subject to the five-year minimum occupation period (MOP).

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second supplementary question is: beyond the so-called natural increase in the number of units that are put up for rent, are there other proactive measures that the Government is taking in order to increase the number of rental flats available for renting, from now until December 2026?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: More details will be shared if there is a written answer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But suffice to say, in general, over the past five years, the proportion of flats rented out and the average number of occupants in each flat type has been fairly stable.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For the second supplementary question, can the Member repeat?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: It is basically that, other than this measure, are there other measures that will be taken to increase the actual units to be supplied?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If we look at the analysts' reports, actually there is a range of views and most of them also cannot find a strong position of whether this will increase the supply because it really depends on whether landlords and tenants take up this additional relaxation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I have looked at some of the analysts' reports.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Some said that,  the supply might actually decline because, for example, if a company is renting out two flats for eight workers and they are renting in two flats now, they may combine, at least for the next few years, into one flat.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, some of the landlords might take advantage of this temporary relaxation to increase the number of tenants in their flat.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, most analysts also cannot project the number of flat supply that may come onstream because of this.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Earlier in my reply, I also mentioned that this move should be seen in the context of the suite of measures that have been put in place: increasing the number of flats available in the market, increasing the number of Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) flats available, the suite of measures that were put in place to moderate the imbalances between demand and supply.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The first one relates to my question in the Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is about how the HDB infrastructure can cope, because going from six to eight, essentially, you are increasing.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If everybody takes it up, it is a third, 33% more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, in the light of the new occupancy guidelines, which may lead to increased usage of infrastructure, who will be responsible for covering the cost associated with a higher maintenance in the enhancement of facilities in affected HDB blocks?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If it is intensified, who is going to bear cost, especially in the common areas?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Actually, I am very happy because I was the one who championed this.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But then, if you are now allowing – at flat level – an intensification of 33% from six to eight, how is it that you can still keep the Singaporean character if everybody decides to increase to the maximum cap?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And of these 58,000 HDB whole flats that are rented out, only 16% are rented out to six unrelated occupants.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, by and large, our neighbourhood estates are still majority owner-occupied.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Again, I also mentioned that we are not sure if all of the tenants and landlords will take full advantage of this relaxation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We do not expect the operation and maintenance costs of common areas and facilities, like lifts and playgrounds, to go up significantly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Like the Member said, most of the users are existing owner-occupiers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just two questions for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I refer to the point the Senior Minister of State made about the non-citizen quota.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand it only applies when the entire flat is rented out and does not apply when bedrooms are rented out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the decision to increase the rental occupancy cap, does HDB actively track, or does it plan to actively track the nationality of tenants who are renting out bedrooms?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And would the Senior Minister of State agree with me, notwithstanding his previous answer to the supplementary question by Member Foo Mee Har, there will also be additional manpower expectations on Town Councils arising from the new rental occupancy cap?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, when you have eight tenants in an HDB flat, they may dry their clothes at the common corridor and there may be additional disamenities of this nature requiring HDB to come in to liaise with the owner and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My Parliamentary Question covered manpower issues and is it the Senior Minister of State's position that there is sufficient manpower for HDB to deal with this problem?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The second question pertains to a possible increase in noise-related complaints with the revised rental occupancy cap.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Community Advisory Panel on Neighbourhood Noise that was set up in 2022, recommended a quantitative noise threshold in the form of decibels to help in the assessment of egregious cases of neighbourhood noise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In January last year, Minister Desmond Lee replied in Parliament that the Ministry of National Development (MND) was studying the recommendations and would provide a response when it was ready.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I inquire whether a decision has been made on the specific proposal pertaining to a quantitative noise threshold and if more communication and education needs to be undertaken by HDB to prospective owners who intend to let out their flats or bedrooms to ensure that tenants adhere to the recommended quiet hours of between 10.00 pm and 8.00 am?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The first one is a relatively factual one, whether the occupancy cap applies to flat or room rentals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It applies to all room rentals, tenant composition and so on.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And that is why we have to also look at these numbers and have an appreciation of whether there will be a sudden explosion of disamenities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But we take all complaints seriously and will continue to work closely with community partners, including Town Councils.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On the Member's second query regarding the quantifiable measure for noise, I invite the Member to file a Parliamentary Question on this because separate data on this is not available to me at this point in time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just a quick follow-up to the reply to the first supplementary question on the applicability of the non-citizen quota vis-à-vis the renting out of bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have the relevant printout from the HDB website here.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It states that the non-citizen quota does not apply to the renting out of bedrooms.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I hope the Senior Minister of State can clarify this particular point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Is that applicable only in a certain situation or is that the broad policy that the quota does not apply to the renting out of bedrooms?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I thought the Member meant the occupancy cap, whether it applies to whole flat rentals or bedroom rentals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For the non-citizen quota, it applies for whole flat rentals.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Speaker, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State for clarifications regarding not the prevention or mitigation of disamenities but what is the recourse available to victims of disamenities caused by – I am going to bring up something other than noise – air-conditioning condensation due to excessive and incessant use of air-conditioning by tenants that creates health hazards in the neighbouring units where residents have to deal with mold and a lot of these things and they have to spend money to repaint and to get rid of this mold.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Is there any recourse for these victims and what does MND intend to do about possibly enhancing some regulations and enforcement actions so that we can prevent such excessive air-conditioning usage by tenants which, anecdotally on the ground, seems to be predominantly an issue with tenanted units.
